PCA itself used none — the components are the same whether or not \(\mathbf{y}\) exists — but the evaluation of how many components to keep for a supervised task necessarily uses the labels, through the cross-validated accuracy. That is legitimate as long as the PCA is refitted inside each fold, as the chunk does.

4.7 Limits of PCA, and t-SNE and UMAP for visualisation

PCA is linear: the components are weighted sums of the features, and the subspace is flat. Data on a curved surface — a spiral, a sphere, the half-moons — are poorly summarised by any flat subspace. Kernel PCA and the autoencoders of Unit 6 are the nonlinear extensions.

More important, and more often forgotten: variance is not information. PCA ranks directions by how much the data spread along them, not by how relevant that spread is to any question. If the difference between two groups lies along a direction of small variance while a large, irrelevant source (age, batch, instrument) dominates, the first components will describe the irrelevant source and the signal will be in a late component or discarded. The chunk builds exactly this situation.

set.seed(0); n <- 300
irrelevant <- rnorm(n, 0, 4)                                  # e.g. patient age: large spread, unrelated to the groups
group <- sample(0:1, n, replace = TRUE)
marker <- ifelse(group == 0, -1, 1) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.4)        # informative feature: small spread, separates the groups
Xvi <- cbind(irrelevant, marker); pv <- prcomp(Xvi); Zvi <- pv$x
cat("proportion of variance:", round(pv$sdev^2 / sum(pv$sdev^2), 3), "| PC1 loadings:", round(pv$rotation[, 1], 3), "\n")
## proportion of variance: 0.928 0.072 | PC1 loadings: -0.999 -0.033
cv_glm <- function(F) { set.seed(0); fo <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n)); mean(sapply(1:5, function(f) {
  tr <- fo != f; m <- glm(group[tr] ~ ., data.frame(F[tr, , drop = FALSE]), family = binomial)
  mean((predict(m, data.frame(F[!tr, , drop = FALSE]), type = "response") > 0.5) == group[!tr]) })) }
cat(sprintf("CV accuracy of logistic regression:  PC1 only = %.3f | PC2 only = %.3f | both features = %.3f\n",
            cv_glm(Zvi[, 1, drop = FALSE]), cv_glm(Zvi[, 2, drop = FALSE]), cv_glm(Xvi)))
## CV accuracy of logistic regression:  PC1 only = 0.570 | PC2 only = 0.997 | both features = 1.000
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1)); gc <- ifelse(group == 0, BLUE, ORANGE)
plot(Xvi, col = gc, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, xlab = "irrelevant feature (variance 16)", ylab = "marker (variance ~1.2)", main = "original features")
plot(Zvi, col = gc, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, xlab = "PC1 (93%)", ylab = "PC2 (7%)", main = "principal components")

Figure 14. Left: two groups (colours hidden from PCA) separated cleanly along a feature of small variance, while an unrelated feature has about fourteen times the variance. Right: PCA puts about 93 % of the variance into PC1, which is essentially the irrelevant feature; the group separation survives only in PC2. An analyst who kept “the component that explains 93 % of the variance” would have discarded the only informative direction — a logistic regression on PC1 alone performs near chance (about 57 %) while one on PC2 alone is nearly perfect, as the printout shows.

For visualisation of high-dimensional data in two dimensions, two nonlinear methods have largely displaced PCA in the biomedical literature: t-SNE,[23] which places points so that neighbours in the original space remain neighbours, and UMAP,[24] which does the same faster and with a stronger claim to preserve coarse structure. Both produce the striking “islands” plots of single-cell RNA sequencing (R packages Rtsne and uwot). Both are for visualisation only: the distances between islands and their sizes are not meaningful, the result depends on tuning parameters and the random seed, and new points cannot be placed without recomputing. They should never be used as preprocessing for clustering or classification, and clusters seen in them should be confirmed in the original feature space.

Common misconception

“The first two components explain only 30 % of the variance, so the PCA failed.” A low proportion in two components means the data are genuinely high-dimensional, which is a finding, not a failure; and, as Figure 14 shows, a high proportion in one component can be a failure, when that component is irrelevant. The proportion of variance measures compression, not relevance.

5. Independent component analysis

5.1 The cocktail-party problem; independence versus uncorrelatedness

Two people speak at once in a room with two microphones. Each microphone records a different weighted sum of the two voices, the weights depending on the distances. Given only the two recordings, can the two voices be recovered? This is the cocktail-party problem, the prototype of blind source separation: \(m\) observed signals \(\mathbf{x}(t)\) are modelled as an unknown linear mixture of \(m\) unknown source signals \(\mathbf{s}(t)\),

\[\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{s}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{s}} = \mathbf{W}\,\mathbf{x}\] where \(\mathbf{A}\) is the \(m \times m\) mixing matrix, and the task is to find an unmixing matrix \(\mathbf{W} \approx \mathbf{A}^{-1}\) from the observations alone, with no knowledge of \(\mathbf{A}\) or of the sources except one assumption: the sources are statistically independent.

Independent component analysis (ICA) is the family of methods that solve this problem. The name and formal definition are due to Comon (1994);[25] the algorithm that made it practical, Infomax, to Bell and Sejnowski (1995);[26] and the fast fixed-point algorithm implemented below, FastICA, to Hyvärinen and Oja, whose 2000 review is the standard introduction.[27]

The distinction that makes ICA different from PCA is between uncorrelated and independent. Two variables are uncorrelated when their covariance is zero — a statement about second moments only. They are independent when their joint distribution factorises, \(p(s_1, s_2) = p(s_1)\,p(s_2)\) — a statement about all moments. Independence implies uncorrelatedness; the converse holds only for Gaussian variables. PCA finds uncorrelated components, and for a Gaussian signal that is all there is to find; for non-Gaussian signals there is a stronger structure, independence, and PCA does not see it.

5.2 Non-Gaussianity as the lever

Why can independence be recovered at all? The argument is the central limit theorem run backwards. A sum of independent random variables is more Gaussian than any of its terms. Each observed mixture \(x_j = \sum_l a_{jl} s_l\) is such a sum, so the mixtures are closer to Gaussian than the sources. Conversely, among all linear combinations \(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}\) of the observations, the least Gaussian ones must be the original sources (up to scale). ICA therefore searches for the directions \(\mathbf{w}\) that maximise a measure of non-Gaussianity, and it works exactly to the extent that the sources are non-Gaussian — at most one source may be Gaussian, or the problem has no unique solution.

Two measures of non-Gaussianity are in use. Kurtosis, the standardised fourth moment \(\kappa = \mathbb{E}[s^4]/\mathbb{E}[s^2]^2 - 3\), is zero for a Gaussian, positive for “peaky” heavy-tailed distributions (speech, spikes) and negative for flat ones (a square wave, a uniform variable); it is simple but sensitive to outliers. Negentropy, the entropy deficit relative to a Gaussian of equal variance, is zero for a Gaussian and positive otherwise, is robust, and is what FastICA approximates with a smooth contrast function such as \(\log\cosh\) (whose derivative is \(\tanh\)). FastICA first whitens the data with PCA (Section 4.5), so that the remaining problem is to find a rotation, then finds the rotation one direction at a time by a fixed-point iteration on the chosen contrast.

5.3 FastICA from scratch on three synthetic sources: PCA fails, ICA succeeds

There is no FastICA in base R, so the chunk implements it from scratch in about twenty lines — centre, whiten via eigen of the covariance, then a fixed-point iteration with \(g = \tanh\) and Gram–Schmidt deflation — exactly as the Python edition wrote its own. Three sources — a sine, a square wave and a sawtooth — are mixed by a random \(3 \times 3\) matrix into three observed channels. PCA and FastICA are each asked for three components, and the recovered components are compared with the true sources by their absolute correlation.

fastica <- function(X, n_comp, max_iter = 200, tol = 1e-6, seed = 1) {
  Xc <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)               # 1. centre
  e  <- eigen(cov(Xc)); K <- diag(1 / sqrt(e$values)) %*% t(e$vectors)   # 2. whitening matrix (PCA)
  Xw <- (Xc %*% t(K))[, 1:n_comp, drop = FALSE]              #    whitened data: identity covariance
  W  <- matrix(0, n_comp, n_comp); set.seed(seed)
  for (i in 1:n_comp) {                                       # 3. one independent direction at a time
    w <- rnorm(n_comp); w <- w / sqrt(sum(w^2))
    for (it in 1:max_iter) {
      wx <- as.vector(Xw %*% w); g <- tanh(wx); gp <- 1 - g^2
      wn <- colMeans(g * Xw) - mean(gp) * w                   #    fixed-point update (negentropy, g = tanh)
      if (i > 1) { Wp <- W[1:(i - 1), , drop = FALSE]; wn <- wn - t(Wp) %*% (Wp %*% wn) }  # deflation
      wn <- as.vector(wn); wn <- wn / sqrt(sum(wn^2))
      if (abs(abs(sum(wn * w)) - 1) < tol) { w <- wn; break }
      w <- wn
    }
    W[i, ] <- w
  }
  list(S = Xw %*% t(W), U = W %*% K[1:n_comp, , drop = FALSE], mu = colMeans(X))   # S = sources; U = full unmixing
}
set.seed(0); tt <- seq(0, 8, length.out = 2000)
saw <- function(x) 2 * (x / (2 * pi) - floor(0.5 + x / (2 * pi)))
S_true <- cbind(sin(2 * pi * tt), sign(sin(2 * pi * 0.6 * tt + 1)), saw(2 * pi * 0.4 * tt))
S_true <- scale(S_true + 0.05 * matrix(rnorm(length(S_true)), ncol = 3))
A_mix  <- matrix(rnorm(9), 3, 3); X_mix <- S_true %*% t(A_mix)
kurt <- function(M) apply(M, 2, function(z) mean(((z - mean(z)) / sd(z))^4) - 3)
cat("kurtosis of the sources :", round(kurt(S_true), 2), " (far from 0: non-Gaussian)\n")
## kurtosis of the sources : -1.49 -1.99 -1.1  (far from 0: non-Gaussian)
cat("kurtosis of the mixtures:", round(kurt(X_mix), 2), " (closer to 0: mixing Gaussianises)\n")
## kurtosis of the mixtures: 0.03 -0.24 -0.94  (closer to 0: mixing Gaussianises)
S_pca <- prcomp(X_mix)$x; S_ica <- fastica(X_mix, 3)$S
mt <- function(R, nm) { C <- abs(cor(S_true, R)); dimnames(C) <- list(c("sine","square","saw"), paste0(nm, 1:3)); round(C, 3) }
cat("\nPCA |correlation| with each source:\n"); print(mt(S_pca, "PC"))
## 
## PCA |correlation| with each source:
##          PC1   PC2   PC3
## sine   0.415 0.198 0.888
## square 0.587 0.793 0.163
## saw    0.753 0.449 0.481
cat("\nICA |correlation| with each source:\n"); print(mt(S_ica, "IC"))
## 
## ICA |correlation| with each source:
##          IC1   IC2   IC3
## sine   0.057 0.998 0.003
## square 1.000 0.000 0.000
## saw    0.165 0.013 0.986

The kurtosis printout shows the central-limit argument at work: every source has a kurtosis well below zero (a sine, a square wave and a sawtooth are all flat-topped), and every mixture is closer to zero. The correlation tables show the result. Each PCA component is a blend of the three sources, with correlations spread across the row (best per source only 0.75–0.89) — PCA has found uncorrelated directions, which is not enough. Each ICA component correlates almost perfectly (above 0.98) with exactly one source and negligibly with the other two: the sources have been recovered without any knowledge of the mixing matrix.

panels <- list(list("true sources s(t)", S_true), list("observed mixtures x(t)", X_mix),
               list("PCA components", S_pca), list("ICA components", S_ica))
par(mfcol = c(3, 4), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1))
for (col in seq_along(panels)) for (row in 1:3) {
  plot(tt, panels[[col]][[2]][, row], type = "l", col = PALETTE[col], lwd = 0.7, xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "")
  if (row == 1) title(panels[[col]][[1]], cex.main = 0.95)
}

Figure 15. Columns: the three sources; the three recorded mixtures, each a weighted sum of all sources; the three principal components, still mixtures (a sine with a square wave superposed, and so on); and the three independent components, which are the sources again — but in a different order and, for some, upside down. Compare the row order of the first and last columns.

The two ambiguities. ICA cannot recover the order of the sources — any permutation of the rows of \(\mathbf{s}\) with the matching permutation of the columns of \(\mathbf{A}\) gives the same \(\mathbf{x}\) — nor their scale and sign, since multiplying a source by \(c\) and its column of \(\mathbf{A}\) by \(1/c\) changes nothing. FastICA fixes the scale by returning unit-variance components and leaves order and sign arbitrary. Consequently the “first independent component” means nothing (unlike the first principal component); components are identified by their content — waveform, spatial pattern, correlation with a reference — and that identification is where the analyst’s knowledge enters.

5.4 Biomedical application: removing an artefact from a multichannel recording

Electrophysiological recordings — the EEG with its 19 to 256 scalp electrodes, the multi-lead ECG, the magnetoencephalogram — are the natural home of ICA, because each electrode records a linear mixture, through the conducting tissues, of several sources: the neural or cardiac activity of interest, and artefacts such as eye blinks, muscle activity, the heartbeat seen by the EEG, electrode drift and mains interference. Makeig and colleagues first applied ICA to EEG in 1996,[28] and Jung and colleagues showed in 2000 that artefact components could be identified and removed — the recording reconstructed from the remaining components — more selectively than by rejecting contaminated epochs or by regression on a reference channel.[29] This ICA-based artefact rejection is today a standard step in EEG preprocessing.

The chunk simulates the situation in miniature: a clean “ECG” source, an eye-blink-like artefact (three slow Gaussian bumps) and a slow baseline drift are mixed into four channels with different weights; FastICA is run with three components; the artefact component is identified by its correlation with the known blink (in practice: by its waveform and its spatial pattern), set to zero, and the channels are reconstructed. Reconstruction needs the Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse of the unmixing matrix, MASS::ginv.[37] The removal is scored by the root-mean-square deviation of each cleaned channel from its blink-free version.

set.seed(0); fs <- 250; tt2 <- seq(0, 10, by = 1 / fs); beats <- seq(0.4, 10, by = 0.8)   # 75 bpm
ecg   <- rowSums(sapply(beats, function(b) exp(-((tt2-b)/.012)^2) - .3*exp(-((tt2-b-.05)/.02)^2) + .25*exp(-((tt2-b+.2)/.06)^2)))
blink <- rowSums(sapply(c(1.5, 4.2, 7.8), function(b) exp(-((tt2-b)/.12)^2)))              # three slow deflections
drift <- 0.3 * sin(2 * pi * 0.2 * tt2)                                                     # respiration-like wander
src <- cbind(ecg, blink, drift)
Mmix <- matrix(c(1,.2,.3, .8,1.2,.2, .6,.6,.5, .3,1.5,.4), 4, 3, byrow = TRUE)             # 4 channels x 3 sources
channels <- src %*% t(Mmix) + 0.03 * matrix(rnorm(length(tt2) * 4), ncol = 4)
clean_target <- channels - outer(blink, Mmix[, 2])                                         # channels without the blink
ic <- fastica(channels, 3, max_iter = 1000, seed = 2)
corr <- abs(cor(src, ic$S)); dimnames(corr) <- list(c("ecg","blink","drift"), paste0("IC", 1:3))
k_art <- which.max(corr["blink", ])                                                        # identify the blink component
S_clean <- ic$S; S_clean[, k_art] <- 0
cleaned <- sweep(S_clean %*% t(MASS::ginv(ic$U)), 2, ic$mu, "+")                            # zero it, reconstruct
rmse <- function(a, b) sqrt(colMeans((a - b)^2))
cat("|corr| of components with (ecg, blink, drift):\n"); print(round(corr, 3))
## |corr| of components with (ecg, blink, drift):
##         IC1   IC2   IC3
## ecg   0.047 0.001 0.975
## blink 0.088 0.989 0.014
## drift 0.921 0.069 0.009
cat(sprintf("\nartefact component identified: IC%d\n", k_art))
## 
## artefact component identified: IC2
print(data.frame(blink_weight = Mmix[, 2], RMSE_before = round(rmse(channels, clean_target), 3),
                 RMSE_after = round(rmse(cleaned, clean_target), 3), row.names = paste0("ch", 1:4)))
##     blink_weight RMSE_before RMSE_after
## ch1          0.2       0.042      0.021
## ch2          1.2       0.255      0.086
## ch3          0.6       0.127      0.046
## ch4          1.5       0.319      0.107
layout(matrix(c(1,5, 2,6, 3,7, 4,8), 4, 2, byrow = TRUE), widths = c(2.2, 1))
par(mar = c(2, 3, 1.5, 1))
for (j in 1:4) {
  plot(tt2, channels[, j], type = "l", col = GREY, lwd = 0.6, xlab = "", ylab = paste0("ch", j), yaxt = "n")
  lines(tt2, cleaned[, j], col = BLUE, lwd = 0.6)
  for (b in c(1.5, 4.2, 7.8)) rect(b - .3, par("usr")[3], b + .3, par("usr")[4], col = rgb(.82,.41,.12,.12), border = NA)
  if (j == 1) legend("topright", c("recorded", "after removing artefact IC"), col = c(GREY, BLUE), lwd = 1.5, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
}
nm <- c("ecg", "blink", "drift")
for (j in 1:3) { plot(tt2, ic$S[, j], type = "l", lwd = 0.6, col = if (j == k_art) ORANGE else GREEN, xlab = "", ylab = paste0("IC", j), yaxt = "n")
                 title(sprintf("IC%d ~ %s", j, nm[which.max(corr[, j])]), cex.main = 0.85) }
plot.new()

Figure 16. Left: the four recorded channels (grey) and the same channels after the artefact component was zeroed and the recording reconstructed (blue). The three shaded intervals mark the blinks; in the recorded channels they appear as slow deflections of varying size — large in channels 2 and 4, which carry the largest blink weight — and in the cleaned channels they are largely gone, while the beats are untouched. Right: the three independent components, one of which (orange) is the blink; the others are the ECG and the drift. The table reports the root-mean-square deviation of each channel from its blink-free version, which falls by a factor of two to three; the residual is the price of imperfect separation in noise and of the sign/scale indeterminacy absorbed into the reconstruction.

Why ICA and not filtering?

A blink and a heartbeat overlap in frequency, so no frequency filter removes one without distorting the other. ICA separates them by a different property — their statistical independence and their different spatial signatures across channels — which is why it needs several channels and a filter needs one. The same logic applies to the removal of the cardiac artefact from EEG, of muscle artefact, and of the maternal ECG from an abdominal fetal ECG recording.

5.5 PCA versus ICA

PCA ICA
Criterion Maximal variance / minimal reconstruction error Maximal statistical independence (non-Gaussianity)
Statistics used Second order only (covariance) Higher order (kurtosis, negentropy)
Components are Uncorrelated and orthogonal Independent; not orthogonal in general
Ordering By variance; the first component is special None; components identified by content
Sign / scale Sign arbitrary; scale \(= \sqrt{\lambda}\) Sign and scale arbitrary (unit variance by convention)
Solution Unique, closed form (eigen / SVD) Iterative; depends on start and contrast; at most one Gaussian source
Typical use Compression, visualisation, noise reduction, preprocessing Blind source separation: EEG/ECG/MEG artefacts, fMRI networks, hyperspectral unmixing
Assumes Linearity; variance = relevance Linearity; independent, non-Gaussian sources; as many channels as sources

6. Other methods, briefly

Gaussian mixture models and the EM algorithm. Model the data as a weighted sum of \(k\) Gaussian densities, \(p(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_j \pi_j\, \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)\), and fit the weights, means and covariances by maximum likelihood. The fitting algorithm is expectation–maximisation (EM),[30] which alternates an E-step — compute, for every point, the posterior probability (responsibility) of each component — and an M-step — re-estimate each component as responsibility-weighted statistics. This is soft k-means exactly: k-means is the limit of EM for Gaussians with equal spherical covariances when the responsibilities are forced to 0 or 1. Because each component has its own covariance, mixtures handle clusters of different size, spread and orientation (the failure of Figure 5a), and the number of components can be chosen by a likelihood criterion (BIC). In R the package mclust provides it.

DBSCAN. Density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise[31] defines a cluster as a maximal set of points connected through regions of high density: a point is a core point if at least minPts points lie within distance eps of it; core points within eps of each other are in the same cluster; non-core points within reach of a core point join it; everything else is labelled noise. It needs no \(k\), finds clusters of any shape, and is the only method here that can refuse to assign a point. Its weaknesses are the sensitivity to eps and its single density scale. The R package dbscan provides it.

Spectral clustering. Build a similarity graph on the points (k-nearest-neighbour or Gaussian-kernel weights), compute the first few eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian, and run k-means on the rows of the eigenvector matrix. The eigenvectors embed the data in a space where connected regions of the graph become compact groups, so k-means can then find clusters of arbitrary shape; the method is a relaxation of the graph-cut problem. It is accurate on moderate \(n\) and expensive beyond, because of the eigen-decomposition.

Neither mclust nor dbscan is preinstalled in this environment, so — as the Python edition would have, had scikit-learn lacked them — the chunk demonstrates the connectivity idea with the two methods that base R does provide: single-linkage hierarchical clustering (Section 3.5) and a from-scratch spectral clustering in a dozen lines. k-means stands in for the centroid-based methods. All three are run on the half-moons.

spectral <- function(X, k, nn = 10) {                     # normalised-Laplacian spectral clustering, from scratch
  D <- as.matrix(dist(X)); n <- nrow(X); sigma <- median(D)
  W <- exp(-D^2 / (2 * sigma^2))
  for (i in 1:n) { th <- sort(D[i, ])[nn + 1]; W[i, D[i, ] > th] <- 0 }   # keep nn nearest neighbours
  W <- pmax(W, t(W)); dg <- rowSums(W)
  L <- diag(n) - diag(1 / sqrt(dg)) %*% W %*% diag(1 / sqrt(dg))          # normalised Laplacian
  U <- eigen(L, symmetric = TRUE)$vectors[, (n - k + 1):n]               # k smallest-eigenvalue vectors
  U <- U / sqrt(rowSums(U^2) + 1e-9); kmeans(U, k, nstart = 10)$cluster
}
set.seed(0); X_mo <- make_moons(300, 0.06); y_mo <- rep(1:2, c(150, 150))
methods <- list("k-means (centroid)" = kmeans(X_mo, 2, nstart = 10)$cluster,
                "single linkage (connectivity)" = cutree(hclust(dist(X_mo), "single"), 2),
                "spectral, 10-NN graph" = spectral(X_mo, 2))
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1))
for (nm in names(methods)) { lab <- methods[[nm]]
  plot(X_mo, col = PALETTE[lab], pch = 19, cex = 0.5, asp = 1, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       main = sprintf("%s\nARI = %.2f", nm, adjusted_rand(y_mo, lab))) }

Figure 17. The two half-moons under three methods. k-means fails (ARI about 0.2): it can only separate with a straight line, and cuts each crescent in half. Single-linkage clustering and the from-scratch spectral clustering both recover the two moons (ARI near 1), because both define clusters through connectivity — chains of nearby points — rather than through distance to a centre. A Gaussian mixture would improve on k-means but still fail (it can only separate with a quadratic curve); DBSCAN would succeed, for the same connectivity reason as the two shown. The lesson is the one of Section 2.7 again: the method encodes an assumption about cluster shape, and the assumption must fit the data.

7. Evaluating unsupervised results

Section 1.2 stated the problem: there is no truth to compare with. Three kinds of evidence substitute for it.

Internal indices measure the geometry of the partition from the data alone. The silhouette (Section 2.6) rewards partitions whose points are closer to their own cluster than to the nearest other. The Davies–Bouldin index[32] is the average, over clusters, of the worst ratio of within-cluster scatter to between-centroid distance, \(\frac{1}{k}\sum_j \max_{l \ne j} \frac{\sigma_j + \sigma_l}{\lVert \boldsymbol{\mu}_j - \boldsymbol{\mu}_l \rVert}\); lower is better and 0 is ideal. All such indices prefer compact, round, well-separated clusters — which means they prefer the clusters that k-means produces, and will rate a correct connectivity-based partition of the half-moons poorly. An internal index measures agreement with a geometric ideal, not correctness.

External indices compare the partition with a reference labelling when one exists. The adjusted Rand index (Section 2.8) counts agreeing pairs with chance correction;[13] the normalised mutual information (NMI) measures how much knowing the cluster tells you about the label, normalised to \([0, 1]\), and is preferred when the numbers of clusters and classes differ. Both are invariant to relabelling.

Stability. A structure that is real should reappear when the sample is perturbed. Re-run the clustering on random subsets and measure the agreement (ARI) between runs; a partition that changes substantially from one half of the data to the other describes the sample, not the population. Stability is necessary, not sufficient: k-means on uniform data is quite stable, and quite meaningless. The chunk computes the three internal and external indices for \(k = 2, \dots, 4\) on the standardised breast-cancer data (silhouette via cluster::silhouette[38]), then measures stability by subsampling.

davies_bouldin <- function(X, lab) { k <- max(lab); cen <- t(sapply(1:k, function(j) colMeans(X[lab == j, , drop = FALSE])))
  s <- sapply(1:k, function(j) mean(sqrt(rowSums(sweep(X[lab == j, , drop = FALSE], 2, cen[j, ])^2))))
  mean(sapply(1:k, function(j) max(sapply(setdiff(1:k, j), function(l) (s[j] + s[l]) / sqrt(sum((cen[j, ] - cen[l, ])^2)))))) }
nmi <- function(a, b) { t <- table(a, b) / length(a); pa <- rowSums(t); pb <- colSums(t)
  H <- function(p) -sum(p[p > 0] * log(p[p > 0])); I <- sum(ifelse(t > 0, t * log(t / outer(pa, pb)), 0)); I / sqrt(H(pa) * H(pb)) }
d_std <- dist(X_std)
idx <- t(sapply(2:6, function(k) { set.seed(0); lab <- kmeans(X_std, k, nstart = 10)$cluster
  c(silhouette = mean(silhouette(lab, d_std)[, 3]), Davies_Bouldin = davies_bouldin(X_std, lab),
    ARI = adjusted_rand(y_hidden, lab), NMI = nmi(y_hidden, lab)) }))
rownames(idx) <- paste0("k=", 2:6); print(round(idx, 3))
##     silhouette Davies_Bouldin   ARI   NMI
## k=2      0.573          0.820 0.836 0.733
## k=3      0.558          1.135 0.821 0.712
## k=4      0.511          1.555 0.762 0.662
## k=5      0.247          1.618 0.420 0.559
## k=6      0.248          1.654 0.401 0.529
set.seed(0)
for (k in c(2, 3, 4)) {
  aris <- sapply(1:20, function(r) {
    i1 <- sample(nrow(X_std), nrow(X_std) / 2); i2 <- sample(nrow(X_std), nrow(X_std) / 2); common <- intersect(i1, i2)
    k1 <- kmeans(X_std[i1, ], k, nstart = 5); k2 <- kmeans(X_std[i2, ], k, nstart = 5)
    p1 <- max.col(-sapply(1:k, function(j) rowSums(sweep(X_std[common, ], 2, k1$centers[j, ])^2)))
    p2 <- max.col(-sapply(1:k, function(j) rowSums(sweep(X_std[common, ], 2, k2$centers[j, ])^2)))
    adjusted_rand(p1, p2) })
  cat(sprintf("stability k=%d: mean ARI between two random halves = %.3f (worst %.3f)\n", k, mean(aris), min(aris)))
}
## stability k=2: mean ARI between two random halves = 0.979 (worst 0.908)
## stability k=3: mean ARI between two random halves = 0.935 (worst 0.816)
## stability k=4: mean ARI between two random halves = 0.942 (worst 0.485)

The indices agree here, which is not the normal case but is instructive. The silhouette and Davies–Bouldin both prefer \(k = 2\); the external indices (ARI, NMI) also peak at \(k = 2\), where the clusters align best with the biopsy, and fall as \(k\) grows because the extra clusters split the diagnosis groups. The stability analysis shows the two-cluster solution is highly reproducible across random halves (mean ARI about 0.98) and that stability decreases with \(k\). On this dataset all three kinds of evidence agree on two clusters — but that agreement is a fact about these 683 cases and these nine features, not a theorem.

7.1 The trap: validating clusters with the features that built them

A common error in the applied literature deserves its own demonstration. Having clustered patients on a set of variables, the analyst tests whether the clusters differ in those variables, finds \(p < 0.001\) everywhere, and reports that the clusters are “statistically distinct”. They are — by construction. k-means chose the partition that maximises the separation of the groups on exactly those variables, so a test of that separation is circular, and it will be significant even when the data contain no structure at all. The chunk applies k-means to pure noise and runs the tests.

set.seed(0)
X_noise <- matrix(rnorm(200 * 10), 200, 10)                 # 200 'patients', 10 'biomarkers', no structure
lab_noise <- kmeans(X_noise, 2, nstart = 10)$cluster
pvals <- sapply(1:10, function(j) t.test(X_noise[lab_noise == 1, j], X_noise[lab_noise == 2, j])$p.value)
cat("cluster sizes:", as.vector(table(lab_noise)), "\n")
## cluster sizes: 86 114
cat("p-values of the 10 between-cluster t-tests on the clustering features:\n", round(pvals, 4), "\n")
## p-values of the 10 between-cluster t-tests on the clustering features:
##  0.7253 3e-04 0.5783 0 0 0 0 0.3034 0.7801 0.3591
cat(sprintf("features 'significant' at p < 0.05: %d of 10 -- in data with no groups\n", sum(pvals < 0.05)))
## features 'significant' at p < 0.05: 5 of 10 -- in data with no groups
X_held <- matrix(rnorm(200 * 10), 200, 10)                  # the honest test: variables NOT used for clustering
p_held <- sapply(1:10, function(j) t.test(X_held[lab_noise == 1, j], X_held[lab_noise == 2, j])$p.value)
cat(sprintf("the same tests on 10 held-out variables: %d of 10 significant (expected about 0.5 by chance)\n", sum(p_held < 0.05)))
## the same tests on 10 held-out variables: 0 of 10 significant (expected about 0.5 by chance)

Half of the ten “biomarkers” differ significantly between two clusters of pure noise, at least one with a vanishingly small \(p\)-value. The remedy is in the last line: validate clusters on information that did not enter their construction — held-out variables, a later clinical outcome, an independent cohort, a response to treatment. The sepsis phenotypes of Section 8 are a model of this: derived from clinical variables at admission, they were validated by their association with mortality and treatment response, neither of which was used to build them.

Bridge to Supplement S1

The circularity here is the unsupervised twin of the leakage of Supplement S1. There, the test set was contaminated by information from training; here, the “test” of the clusters is contaminated by the clustering. The cure is the same: keep the evidence used to build a result apart from the evidence used to judge it.

8. Medical applications

Patient subtyping: sepsis phenotypes. Sepsis is a syndrome, not a disease, and trials of targeted therapies have repeatedly failed on heterogeneous populations. Seymour and colleagues applied consensus k-means to 29 routinely available clinical and laboratory variables measured within six hours of hospital presentation in 20,189 patients, and identified four phenotypes — α, β, γ and δ — with different organ-dysfunction patterns, biomarker profiles and 28-day mortality (from about 2 % in α to about 32 % in δ); the phenotypes were reproduced in a second cohort of 43,086 patients and, in simulations of three completed trials, the apparent treatment effect changed with the phenotype mix.[33] This is the use case of Section 1.2 in its purest form: no label existed, clustering proposed one, and external evidence — outcomes and treatment response, not the clustering variables — validated it.

Molecular subtypes of tumours. The clustered heatmap of Section 3.6 defined a field. Perou and colleagues applied hierarchical clustering to the expression of some 8,000 genes in 65 breast-tumour samples and found that the tumours fell into groups — later named luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched and basal-like — that differed in their expression patterns and, as later work showed, in prognosis and response to therapy;[34] these “intrinsic subtypes” are now part of clinical practice. A year earlier, Golub and colleagues had shown on acute leukaemias that unsupervised clustering of expression profiles rediscovered the distinction between acute myeloid and acute lymphoblastic leukaemia without being told it (class discovery), and that a supervised classifier could then assign new patients to the classes (class prediction) — the two halves of the pipeline this unit and the previous ones describe.[35]

Population structure with PCA. Genotype data — hundreds of thousands of single-nucleotide polymorphisms per person — are the largest routine application of PCA in biomedicine. Novembre and colleagues computed the first two principal components of the genotypes of 3,000 Europeans and found that the resulting scatter plot reproduced the map of Europe: the two components were, to a close approximation, latitude and longitude of the individuals’ ancestry.[36] The practical consequence is that the leading principal components are included as covariates in every genome-wide association study to prevent ancestry from confounding the association between genotype and disease — PCA as a tool for removing structure rather than for finding it.

Reading an unsupervised-learning paper

Workshop 3 asks you to answer a questionnaire on unsupervised methods; the questions to ask of any paper that uses them are the ones this unit has rehearsed. Which features were clustered, and were they standardised? Which method and which distance, and what shape of cluster does that method assume? How was \(k\) chosen, and how sensitive is the result to it? How stable is the partition under resampling? And, above all, what evidence external to the clustering variables shows that the clusters mean something? A paper that validates its clusters only with the variables that built them has demonstrated Section 7.1, not a discovery.

9. Summary

You should now be able to explain, without notes:

  • What unsupervised learning is, the three tasks it comprises (clustering, dimensionality reduction, density estimation), and why its results cannot be validated the way a classifier’s can.
  • The k-means objective — the within-cluster sum of squares — and why minimising it favours round clusters of similar size and spread.
  • Lloyd’s algorithm (initialise, assign, update, repeat), why each step decreases the objective, why it reaches a local minimum, and what k-means++ and restarts do about it.
  • The variants: fuzzy c-means (membership degrees), k-medoids (a real case as representative; any dissimilarity; robust), mini-batch (scale), k-means++ (seeding), spherical (cosine distance) — and when each is called for.
  • How to choose \(k\) with the elbow, the silhouette and the gap statistic, and why the gap statistic alone can answer “one cluster”.
  • The three failure modes of k-means (unequal sizes, non-convex shapes, unscaled features) and the remedy for each — and why, on the commensurable nine-feature breast-cancer data, the scaling remedy barely changes the result.
  • Why the 96 % agreement between k-means clusters and the biopsy is not an accuracy, and what clustering is for when labels do not exist.
  • The agglomerative algorithm, the four linkage rules and their formulas, the chaining effect of single linkage, how to cut a dendrogram, and what the cophenetic correlation measures.
  • The clustered heatmap of Eisen et al. and how it is built (average linkage, correlation distance, both axes).
  • PCA as variance maximisation and as minimum reconstruction error; how to compute components from the covariance matrix by hand; the scree plot, loadings and biplot; why standardisation comes first; PCA as SVD; whitening.
  • Why variance is not information, and what t-SNE and UMAP are (and are not) for.
  • ICA as blind source separation: independence versus uncorrelatedness, non-Gaussianity as the lever, the permutation and scale ambiguities, and artefact removal by zeroing a component.
  • Gaussian mixtures as soft k-means fitted by EM; DBSCAN and spectral clustering as connectivity-based methods.
  • Internal and external indices, stability, and the circularity of validating clusters with the variables that built them.

10. Self-assessment

  1. A colleague reports that k-means on 25 laboratory variables “achieved 88 % accuracy” in separating diabetic from non-diabetic patients. State two things that are wrong with the sentence.
k-means does not use labels, so it has no accuracy — the 88 % is agreement with a label after relabelling the clusters, and reflects that the diabetes-related variation happens to dominate those 25 variables. And the clusters are named 1 and 2 by the algorithm; the mapping to “diabetic” was chosen to maximise the agreement, which inflates it (with two clusters, the agreement cannot be below 50 %).
  1. Execute by hand one iteration of Lloyd’s algorithm on the points \((0, 0), (0, 2), (5, 0), (5, 2)\) with initial centroids \((0, 0)\) and \((0, 2)\). What happens, and what does it illustrate?
Assignment: \((0,0) \to \mu_1\); \((0,2) \to \mu_2\); \((5,0)\): \(d^2 = 25\) vs \(29 \to \mu_1\); \((5,2)\): \(29\) vs \(25 \to \mu_2\). Update: \(\mu_1 = (2.5, 0)\), \(\mu_2 = (2.5, 2)\). The next assignment changes nothing, so it converges with \(J = 4 \times 6.25 = 25\) — but the partition \(\{(0,0),(0,2)\}, \{(5,0),(5,2)\}\) has \(J = 4\). A poor start led to a local minimum; k-means++ would almost surely have chosen two far-apart initial points.
  1. Why does the elbow method always produce a decreasing curve, and why can the gap statistic return \(k = 1\) while the silhouette cannot?
Adding a centroid can never increase the minimum within-cluster sum of squares (the previous solution is still available), so \(J^\ast(k)\) is non-increasing and reaches 0 at \(k = n\). The silhouette needs at least two clusters to define \(b(i)\), so it cannot evaluate \(k = 1\); the gap statistic compares \(\log J^\ast(k)\) with its value on structureless reference data and can find that no \(k > 1\) improves on \(k = 1\) beyond what uniform noise would.
  1. On the Python edition’s 30-feature data, raw k-means gave a much worse ARI than standardised; on this edition’s 9-feature data it barely changed. Explain both.
Euclidean distance is dominated by the features with the largest numerical range. In the 30-feature data one feature (worst area, in µm²) had values in the thousands and swamped the others, so the raw partition was effectively a threshold on area. The nine mlbench features are all cytological scores on the same 1–10 scale, so no feature can dominate, and standardising changes almost nothing. Standardising is still good practice because it costs nothing and protects against the first situation.
  1. Clusters \(A = \{(0,0), (0,1)\}\) and \(B = \{(3,0), (4,1)\}\). Compute \(D(A, B)\) under single, complete and average linkage.
The four point distances are \(d((0,0),(3,0)) = 3\), \(d((0,0),(4,1)) = \sqrt{17} \approx 4.12\), \(d((0,1),(3,0)) = \sqrt{10} \approx 3.16\), \(d((0,1),(4,1)) = 4\). Single: \(3\). Complete: \(4.12\). Average: \((3 + 4.12 + 3.16 + 4)/4 \approx 3.57\).
  1. A dendrogram built with single linkage on patient data shows one cluster that absorbs almost everyone and a few singletons, however it is cut. What is happening and what would you try?
Chaining: a few intermediate patients bridge the groups, and single linkage follows the bridge, merging the groups before they are complete, while isolated outliers remain as singletons. Try complete, average or Ward linkage, which require the whole clusters to be close; or remove outliers first; or use DBSCAN, which labels sparse points as noise rather than forcing them into clusters.
  1. Compute by hand the principal components of the covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) and the proportion of variance explained by the first.
\(\det(\mathbf{S} - \lambda \mathbf{I}) = (3 - \lambda)^2 - 1 = 0\) gives \(\lambda_1 = 4\), \(\lambda_2 = 2\). For \(\lambda_1 = 4\): \(-w_1 + w_2 = 0\), so \(\mathbf{w}_1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt{2}\); for \(\lambda_2 = 2\), \(\mathbf{w}_2 = (1, -1)/\sqrt{2}\). Proportion explained by PC1: \(4 / 6 \approx 0.667\).
  1. On the nine-feature breast-cancer data the first standardised component explains about 66 % of the variance and loads almost equally on eight features. What does that tell you biologically?
The eight cytological scores are strongly positively correlated: a malignant nucleus tends to be abnormal on all of them at once, so a single “degree of abnormality” axis accounts for two thirds of the variation. PC1 is essentially the average of those eight scores, and it is also the axis along which benign and malignant cases separate — which is why one principal component already classifies the cases at about 97 % (Figure 13).
  1. In the k-NN cross-validation of Section 4.6 the PCA was refitted in every fold even though PCA uses no labels. Why is the precaution necessary?
Fitting PCA on all cases, including the test fold, lets the test cases influence the components (their means and directions), so the test fold is no longer independent of the preprocessing — leakage without labels. The effect is usually small for PCA but can be large for other unsupervised preprocessing (variance-based feature selection, imputation), and the principle is the same as in Supplement S1: every step that learns from data must see only the training fold.
  1. The first ICA component of an EEG recording is sometimes the eye-blink artefact and sometimes not. Why, and how is the artefact component identified in practice?
ICA has a permutation ambiguity: the order of the components is arbitrary and changes with the initialisation. The artefact component is identified by its content — a waveform with large, slow deflections time-locked to blinks, a spatial pattern (the unmixing-matrix row) concentrated on the frontal electrodes, and, if available, a high correlation with the electro-oculogram channel — not by its position.
  1. Two recorded signals are mixtures of two Gaussian sources. Can ICA separate them? Can PCA? Explain.
Neither. For Gaussian variables, uncorrelatedness is independence, and any rotation of two independent Gaussians yields two other independent Gaussians, so the sources are not identifiable: there is no non-Gaussianity for ICA to maximise. PCA returns uncorrelated components, but these are one arbitrary rotation among infinitely many equally “independent” ones. ICA requires that at most one source be Gaussian.
  1. An author clusters patients with k-means on a matrix \(X\), then reports that all variables of \(X\) differ significantly between clusters 1 and 2 \((p < 0.001)\) and concludes the clusters are real. What is wrong, and what would be acceptable evidence?
The tests are circular: k-means chose the partition that maximises the separation of the clusters on exactly those columns of \(X\), so significant differences are guaranteed even in pure noise (Section 7.1). Acceptable evidence is external to the clustering variables: differences in a held-out variable or a later outcome, reproduction of the clusters in an independent cohort, stability under resampling, or an association with treatment response, as in the sepsis-phenotype study.

Glossary

Adjusted Rand index (ARI)
External index comparing two partitions by the pairs of cases they agree to group or separate, corrected for chance: 0 for a random partition, 1 for identical partitions; invariant to relabelling.
Agglomerative clustering
Bottom-up hierarchical clustering: start with one cluster per point and repeatedly merge the two closest clusters according to a linkage rule (R: hclust).
Blind source separation
Recovering unknown source signals from observed mixtures without knowing the mixing process; ICA is the main method.
Chaining
The tendency of single linkage to merge clusters through chains of intermediate points, producing elongated clusters.
Cophenetic distance / correlation
The height at which two points are first joined in a dendrogram / the correlation between cophenetic and original distances, measuring how faithfully the tree represents the data (R: cophenetic).
Covariance matrix
The \(p \times p\) symmetric matrix of feature variances (diagonal) and covariances (off-diagonal); its eigenvectors are the principal components.
Dendrogram
The tree produced by hierarchical clustering; leaves are cases, internal nodes are merges, and the height of a node is the distance at which the merge occurred.
Eigenvector / eigenvalue
A vector \(\mathbf{w}\) with \(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{w} = \lambda\mathbf{w}\); for a covariance matrix, a direction of variation and the variance along it (R: eigen).
Explained variance
The fraction \(\lambda_j / \sum_l \lambda_l\) of total variance carried by principal component \(j\).
FastICA
Fixed-point ICA algorithm that whitens the data and then finds directions of maximal non-Gaussianity one at a time; implemented from scratch in Section 5.3.
Gap statistic
Criterion for \(k\) comparing the observed \(\log J^\ast(k)\) with its expectation on structureless reference data; can select \(k = 1\).
Gaussian mixture model
Density model as a weighted sum of Gaussians, fitted by EM; its components are soft clusters with their own covariance (R: mclust).
Independent component analysis (ICA)
Linear decomposition into statistically independent components, found by maximising non-Gaussianity; determined only up to permutation, sign and scale.
k-means++
Initialisation that chooses successive centroids with probability proportional to their squared distance from the centroids already chosen.
Kurtosis / negentropy
Measures of non-Gaussianity: the standardised fourth moment minus 3 / the entropy deficit relative to a Gaussian of equal variance.
Linkage
The rule defining the distance between two clusters from the distances between their points: single (min), complete (max), average (mean), Ward (increase in within-cluster sum of squares).
Lloyd’s algorithm
The alternating assignment/update procedure that minimises the k-means objective to a local minimum.
Loading
The weight of an original feature in a principal component (an entry of the eigenvector).
Medoid
The data point of a cluster with smallest total dissimilarity to the other members; the representative used by k-medoids/PAM (R: cluster::pam).
Principal component analysis (PCA)
Orthogonal linear transformation to uncorrelated components ordered by variance; equivalently, the subspace of minimum reconstruction error (R: prcomp).
Silhouette
For a point, \((b - a)/\max(a, b)\) where \(a\) is its mean distance to its own cluster and \(b\) to the nearest other; averaged over points, an internal index (R: cluster::silhouette).
Singular value decomposition (SVD)
Factorisation \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^\top\); the right singular vectors are the principal components and \(\sigma_j^2/(n-1)\) the eigenvalues.
Unsupervised learning
Learning from a data matrix without labels: finding groups, low-dimensional summaries or a density.
Whitening
Transforming data to identity covariance (uncorrelated, unit-variance components); the first step of FastICA.
Within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS)
\(\sum_j \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in C_j} \lVert \mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j \rVert^2\); the k-means objective (R: kmeans()$tot.withinss).

Textbooks & resources

  • James G, Witten D, Hastie T, Tibshirani R. An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R. 2nd ed. Springer; 2021 — Chapter 12, PCA and clustering with R labs; the R companion to the whole course. Free PDF at statlearning.com.
  • Hastie T, Tibshirani R, Friedman J. The Elements of Statistical Learning. 2nd ed. Springer; 2009 — Chapter 14, “Unsupervised learning”: cluster analysis, PCA, ICA, the gap statistic. Free PDF.
  • Venables WN, Ripley BD. Modern Applied Statistics with S (MASS). 4th ed. Springer; 2002 — the reference for the R functions used here.
  • Hyvärinen A, Karhunen J, Oja E. Independent Component Analysis. Wiley; 2001 — the reference monograph on ICA.
  • Kassambara A. Practical Guide to Cluster Analysis in R. STHDA; 2017 — factoextra, cluster and NbClust for the methods of Sections 2–3.
